rst-1-hyg-01.title: Recognize food poisoning and food hazards
rst-1-hyg-01.objective: Classify the causes that make food unsafe, stop using affected items when you find a problem, and report it.

paragraphs.knowledge: Food hazards are not limited to bacteria and viruses. Parasites, chemicals such as detergents and pesticides, and objects such as metal and glass can also harm health. Food is not necessarily safe just because it looks and smells normal. Checks are needed at receiving, storage, preparation, and service.
paragraphs.procedure: Before starting, consider what might get into the food. If you notice damaged packaging, chemicals stored in the wrong place, or chipped utensils, separate the affected items from other food and stop using them. Tell the person in charge the product name, quantity, location, and time of discovery. Do not serve the items until a decision has been made.
paragraphs.mistakes: It is wrong to assume that heating later will make everything safe. Normal heating cannot remove chemicals or glass. Do not taste food of unknown safety to check it, or remove only the suspect part and serve the rest.
paragraphs.scenario: A container on the preparation counter smells of detergent. A clear liquid cannot be assumed to be seasoning. Isolate the container and report whether it may have contacted nearby dishes. Follow the person in charge, who checks the scope of the impact before deciding whether dishes must be remade.

rst-1-hyg-01.summary: Consider the type of hazard, do not serve suspect food, and report specific facts.
rst-1-hyg-01.activity: For bacteria, detergent, and glass, explain one way each could get into food and one way to prevent it.

rst-1-hyg-02.title: Keep bacteria off food, limit growth, and reduce them
rst-1-hyg-02.objective: Apply the three principles for preventing bacterial food poisoning throughout a sequence of work.

paragraphs.knowledge: Combine keeping bacteria off food, preventing them from multiplying in food, and reducing them through appropriate heating or other suitable methods. Handwashing and separate utensils help keep bacteria off food. Cold storage and time control limit growth. Necessary heating is the step for killing them.
paragraphs.procedure: Take only the quantity needed out of the refrigerator and prepare it with utensils designated for that purpose. Next, heat the food using an appropriate method and plate it with clean utensils. Check hands and utensils when changing tasks, and keep food that must wait at its designated storage temperature.
paragraphs.mistakes: Refrigeration and freezing do not kill all bacteria. Storage limits must still be followed at low temperatures. Gripping thoroughly cooked meat with tongs used for raw meat may contaminate the food again after cooking.
paragraphs.scenario: The person cooking meat tries to use one pair of tongs for both raw meat and plating. Attention is needed not only to cooking but also to contamination afterward. Speak to the worker and have them switch to clean serving utensils.

rst-1-hyg-02.summary: Use the three principles together from receiving to service, rather than treating them as separate slogans.
rst-1-hyg-02.activity: Draw the workflow for a chicken dish and write in actions that correspond to each of the three principles.

rst-2-hyg-01.title: Make the HACCP plan work on the floor
rst-2-hyg-01.objective: Connect general hygiene controls with control of critical process steps, and explain decisions after deviations and verification.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Connect the seven principles into one process
paragraphTitles.scenario: When the same temperature keeps appearing

paragraphs.knowledge: Food hygiene aims to prevent harm to health caused by food. When reading incident examples or statistics, check the reporting year and distinguish causes with many incidents from causes with many patients. In the restaurant, identify hazards involving ingredients, workers, utensils, temperature, and time, and combine general hygiene management with control of critical process steps.
paragraphs.procedure: Analyze hazards and identify the steps that need particular control. Set the criteria to meet, the monitoring methods, and the actions to take when criteria are not met. Also establish how to check whether the plan is effective and prepare records. Small restaurants can use verified guidance appropriate to their operation, specifying who is responsible, how often to check, and whom to report to.
paragraphs.mistakes: Measuring temperature during cooking checks whether the process meets the criteria at that moment. Verification is when the person in charge reviews records and work to judge whether the measuring method and the plan itself are effective. Filled-in record sheets alone do not prove that work was safe.
paragraphs.scenario: Ono, the person in charge, notices that exactly the same temperature is recorded each time for different dishes. Before blaming the recorder, Ono asks them to demonstrate the measurement and checks the measuring position and recording time. Service decisions for unverified dishes are put on hold. Ono retrains staff on measurement and follows up on implementation the next day.

rst-2-hyg-01.summary: Manage criteria, on-the-floor monitoring, actions after deviations, and verification of the plan as distinct tasks.
rst-2-hyg-01.activity: 30-minute study: read for 8 minutes. Spend 7 minutes drawing the curry process from receiving to service and adding hazards and controls. Explain for 8 minutes who stops what after a deviation; use the last 7 minutes to check records and verification methods.

rst-2-hyg-02.title: Manage a 5S and facility-cleaning plan
rst-2-hyg-02.objective: Prioritize contamination sources inside and outside the facility, and assign daily and periodic cleaning.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Match each place to a cleaning frequency
paragraphTitles.scenario: When foreign matter appears despite a cleaning check

paragraphs.knowledge: Sorting means removing unnecessary items; setting in order means deciding where needed items belong and in what quantity; cleaning means removing dirt. Cleanliness is the maintained result, and building habits means teaching staff to repeat these practices. Food remains and standing water can cause pests, microbial growth, and falls.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the daily condition of floors, drains, grease traps, and toilets. Include hoods, ventilation openings, lighting, refrigerator seals, and storage areas in periodic work according to dirt and usage. Damaged windows or delivery entrances and poor drainage require repairs, not cleaning alone. Ask contractors who can work safely to handle high places or specialized equipment.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not share cleaning tools between toilets and the kitchen. Wash the tools themselves after use and let them dry. Do not place brushes and mops directly on the floor; store them in a designated place where they cannot contaminate food. Keep animals out of food-handling areas. Even businesses where customers interact with animals in the dining area need separation from the kitchen and storage areas.
paragraphs.scenario: The dining area passed its cleaning check, but dust fell from above the serving hatch. The supervisor concludes that shelves above eye level and ventilation openings were missing from the plan. Food is protected and specialist cleaning arranged. A separate person is assigned to check completion, and the next scheduled date and inspection photographs are added to the cleaning sheet.

rst-2-hyg-02.summary: Include upper and surrounding parts of equipment, damage, and tool storage in the cleaning plan, not just visible floors.
rst-2-hyg-02.activity: Read for 8 minutes; draw a simple kitchen plan for 7 minutes; assign daily, weekly, and as-needed cleaning for 8 minutes; spend 7 minutes presenting post-cleaning checks and the reporting route for repairs.

rst-2-hyg-03.title: Choose and handle cleaning chemicals safely
rst-2-hyg-03.objective: Choose cleaning products according to dirt and material, and correct problems with labels, dilution, and storage.

paragraphTitles.procedure: Turn product conditions into work instructions
paragraphTitles.scenario: When an unlabelled bottle is found

paragraphs.knowledge: When food residues remain, microorganisms can use them as nutrients and form a film that is difficult to remove. Cleaning removes dirt and has a different purpose from disinfection. Choose among neutral detergents, alkaline cleaners for grease, and acidic cleaners for scale after checking the object and its material.
paragraphs.procedure: The person in charge checks each product’s purpose, dilution method, protective equipment, and rinsing method against its label and instructions. Even cleaners permitted for use on food have specified targets and conditions of use. Use dedicated containers when transferring chemicals, clearly label the contents, and store them away from food and dishes. Separate cleaning work so splashes cannot reach finished food.
paragraphs.mistakes: Making a solution stronger without authorization can cause residues, material damage, and harm to workers. Mixing an acidic cleaner with sodium hypochlorite risks producing toxic chlorine gas. Prohibit transfer into beverage containers, removal of labels, and dilution by eye. Do not use a container with unknown contents.
paragraphs.scenario: A new worker mistakes a clear liquid for water and puts it on the preparation counter. The person in charge stops its use, isolates it, and checks where the container came from. If it may already have been used on food, the affected food is held and not served until safety is established. Dedicated containers and measuring tools are provided, and all staff demonstrate that they check labels.

rst-2-hyg-03.summary: Check a cleaner’s purpose, concentration, compatible materials, and rinsing conditions, and manage it clearly separately from food.
rst-2-hyg-03.activity: Spend 8 minutes reading product labels, 7 minutes choosing cleaners and protective equipment for three hypothetical types of dirt, 7 minutes designing a label for a transferred chemical, and 8 minutes explaining stopping, isolating, and reporting after incorrect use is found.

rst-1-hyg-03.title: Connect common bacteria with the foods involved
rst-1-hyg-03.objective: Understand where common bacteria come from and choose prevention according to the food and task.

paragraphs.knowledge: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Campylobacter, and Salmonella are associated with foods such as meat and eggs. Bacillus cereus requires attention in foods such as grains, and Clostridium perfringens in the management of curry and simmered dishes. Staphylococcus aureus can transfer to food from human skin or wounds, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus from seafood.
paragraphs.procedure: Wash hands before and after handling raw meat or eggs and use separate utensils. Protect wounds and reassign tasks when appropriate. When storing cooked food, follow the cooling and storage methods specified for each food. Check seafood quality and storage conditions, and carry out necessary washing and heating.
paragraphs.mistakes: Memorizing bacterial names alone does not prevent incidents at work. Bacteria cannot be identified by sight, and having had no problem the previous day is not proof of safety. Do not rely only on normal heating; control temperature, time, and contamination routes.
paragraphs.scenario: A large pot of simmered food has been left at room temperature after closing. Planning to boil it again the next morning does not remove the problem in the storage process. Check how long it has been in that condition, stop using it, and report to the person in charge.

rst-1-hyg-03.summary: Be able to explain not only the foods involved but also which controls are needed for hands, heating, cooling, and storage.
rst-1-hyg-03.activity: Group the bacteria mentioned in the text by their sources in food, people, or the environment, and explain the measures for each aloud.

rst-1-hyg-04.title: Watch for viruses, parasites, and histamine
rst-1-hyg-04.objective: Explain why hazards other than bacteria cannot be assessed through ordinary heating or refrigeration alone.

paragraphs.knowledge: Norovirus can spread not only through bivalve shellfish but also through the feces or vomit of an infected person. Anisakis is a parasite found in seafood. Poorly stored red-fleshed fish and similar foods can cause histamine food poisoning. Each hazard needs its own measures.
paragraphs.procedure: Check your health and wash hands thoroughly, including after using the toilet. Put fish into storage promptly after receiving it, and handle removal of internal organs and visual inspection appropriately. Measures indicated for Anisakis include freezing at −20℃ for at least 24 hours, or heating to at least 70℃, or heating at 60℃ for at least 1 minute. Follow the restaurant’s procedure so the conditions are met through to the center of the fish.
paragraphs.mistakes: The standard temperature for a refrigerator is not the same as the freezing conditions needed against parasites. Do not decide for yourself that marinating in vinegar completes parasite prevention. It is also important not to apply ordinary meat-cooking conditions unchanged to virus control for bivalve shellfish.
paragraphs.scenario: A delivery of red-fleshed fish has been left at room temperature for a long time. Do not assume it can be used simply because it will be chilled now. Tell the person in charge its history and condition. Chilling it afterward is different from eliminating hazards that have already developed.

rst-1-hyg-04.summary: Distinguish the conditions for each hazard; stop using an item and check when unsure.
rst-1-hyg-04.activity: For norovirus, Anisakis, and histamine, explain one difference each in their main preventive measures.

rst-1-hyg-05.title: Receive ingredients at delivery
rst-1-hyg-05.objective: Check both the order and hygienic condition, and identify nonconforming items.

paragraphs.knowledge: Receiving is more than counting quantities. Accepting the wrong product, torn packaging, expired items, or food outside its specified storage conditions affects later preparation. It is important to stop questionable quality or safety at the receiving stage.
paragraphs.procedure: Compare product names and quantities with the order, and check packaging, appearance, odor, dates, and storage instructions. Check chilled and frozen items’ temperatures by the designated method, minimize time at room temperature, and put them away. Separate nonconforming items, obtain instructions such as return arrangements, and record the action.
paragraphs.mistakes: A use-by date and a best-before date do not mean the same thing. An infrared thermometer primarily measures surface temperature. Do not treat a different measurement method as giving an equivalent result, or overlook signs that frozen products have thawed.
paragraphs.scenario: Meat for a reserved meal arrives with a torn edge on the bag. Even when busy, do not transfer it to another container and finish accepting it; separate the damaged item. Tell the relevant staff about the replacement needed and the impact on preparation.

rst-1-hyg-05.summary: Check conformity with the order and hygienic condition; do not mix suspect items with normal stock.
rst-1-hyg-05.activity: Role-play the delivery worker and receiving worker, and practice checking and reporting when damaged packaging is found.

rst-2-hyg-04.title: Check disinfection effectiveness and storage
rst-2-hyg-04.objective: Select disinfection appropriate to the item and prevent recontamination from cleaning until the next use.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Conditions that allow disinfection to work
paragraphTitles.procedure: Check the full path from cleaning to storage
paragraphTitles.mistakes: How clean utensils are placed also matters
paragraphTitles.scenario: Items are wet even after going into the cabinet

paragraphs.knowledge: Disinfection effectiveness depends on whether dirt has first been removed, the chemical type and concentration, contact time, temperature, and the object’s shape. Heat, chemicals, and ultraviolet light cannot all be used in the same way. Check the material and heat resistance, and define a method consistent with the instructions for the utensils and disinfection equipment.
paragraphs.procedure: The person in charge checks cleaning, rinsing, necessary disinfection, drying, and storage as one continuous process. When using alcohol, watch for dilution caused by water on the item. With chlorine-based products, follow treatment requirements appropriate to the product instructions and material. In ultraviolet storage cabinets, avoid stacking that blocks the light, and return utensils to a clean storage area.
paragraphs.mistakes: Stacking washed bowls while wet leaves water at the bottom. Allow knives and cutting boards to dry rather than pressing them against a wall. Put them in a cabinet with doors; keep large utensils in a clean place protected from foreign matter and splashes. Do not let dirty hands or cleaning tools touch disinfected utensils.
paragraphs.scenario: A worker packs dishes into a cabinet and removes them while some remain wet. The supervisor puts their use on hold and checks the stacking, operating conditions, and utensil materials. The items are reprocessed in an appropriate load and the outcome checked. Storage capacity and cleaning assignments are reviewed so the system also works during busy periods.

rst-2-hyg-04.summary: Disinfection is not the end of the process; maintain its effect through drying and storage.
rst-2-hyg-04.activity: Read for 8 minutes; spend 7 minutes organizing treatment steps for two types of utensils and 7 minutes correcting examples of improper storage. In the final 8 minutes, explain why you chose chemicals, heat, or ultraviolet light.

rst-2-hyg-05.title: Maintain instruments and handwashing facilities
rst-2-hyg-05.objective: Check the reliability of readings and the usability of handwashing facilities, and act on faults rather than leaving them unresolved.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Readings need the backing of inspections
paragraphTitles.procedure: Separate daily checks from replacement schedules
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not compensate for missing supplies with personal effort

paragraphs.knowledge: If a probe thermometer reads incorrectly, you cannot judge safety even when you believe food has been heated properly. Check thermometer accuracy regularly and record the date, method, and result. Also check chemical concentrations in disinfection systems and operating hours and replacement history for ultraviolet equipment. Do not assume that a light being on proves effectiveness.
paragraphs.procedure: At opening, check for damage, faulty displays, and missing supplies; assign staff and due dates for periodic inspections separately. Equip handwashing areas with soap, a clean way to dry hands, and bins that will not dirty hands after washing. Check splashes toward food and the direction of hand-dryer airflow, and display instructions clearly. If nailbrushes are used, prevent contamination through sharing or storage.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not dry hands on uniforms because paper towels have run out, or use the handwashing area to store ingredients. Choosing whichever thermometer reading is more convenient when results are doubtful is also dangerous. Identify and stop using instruments that fail inspection, and make decisions using a verified alternative.
paragraphs.scenario: Two thermometers give different readings on the same item. The person in charge standardizes the measuring position and method and checks accuracy according to the instructions. Records for dishes measured with the suspect instrument are reviewed, and service decisions are put on hold until safety can be established. Repairs or replacement and the next inspection date are recorded.

rst-2-hyg-05.summary: Reliable instruments and usable facilities support hygienic behavior on the floor.
rst-2-hyg-05.activity: Read for 8 minutes; create an opening checklist for 7 minutes; practice decisions after thermometer disagreement for 8 minutes; inspect recontamination routes around the handwashing area for 7 minutes.

rst-1-hyg-06.title: Inspect refrigerators and freezers
rst-1-hyg-06.objective: Check the internal temperature, storage dates, and action after a problem as one continuous process.

paragraphs.knowledge: Refrigerators and freezers do not automatically make the food placed in them safe. Check their internal temperature, food dates, and storage arrangement. The source gives examples of control at 10℃ or below for refrigeration and −15℃ or below for freezing; if the food label or restaurant standards are stricter, follow those requirements.
paragraphs.procedure: Read the thermometer at the designated time and record the reading, including its unit and sign. Check dates and packaging, and store items without blocking airflow. Report any reading outside the criteria to the person in charge and obtain instructions on the food and inspection of the equipment.
paragraphs.mistakes: Looking only at the temperature setting does not check the actual temperature inside. Do not erase abnormal readings and record only normal ones, or assume all food can be used after chilling it again. How long the abnormal condition lasted is also important.
paragraphs.scenario: At opening, the internal temperature is above the restaurant’s upper limit. Do not simply shut the door and leave it there: record the time and temperature and report it. Check the previous record and the food’s condition. Do not serve the affected food until a decision is made on whether it can be used.

rst-1-hyg-06.summary: Check measured readings and dates, and retain abnormal readings together with the action taken.
rst-1-hyg-06.activity: Create a refrigerator checklist and write an example record for a day when an abnormal temperature is found.

rst-1-hyg-07.title: Arrange storage and separate utensils to prevent cross-contamination
rst-1-hyg-07.objective: Break the routes by which contamination travels from raw ingredients to prepared food.

paragraphs.knowledge: Juices from raw meat and fish, hands, cutting boards, and knives can transfer dirt or bacteria to other food. Distinguishing food before heating, food after heating, and food eaten raw is fundamental. Food can be contaminated through shared utensils even without direct contact between foods.
paragraphs.procedure: Keep raw meat and fish in covered containers and in positions where their juices cannot drip onto other food. Select utensils according to the food type and purpose, and clean and disinfect them after use. Inspect storage locations and utensils, and redo cleaning before starting if dirt remains.
paragraphs.mistakes: A cutting board with only the visible meat pieces wiped away is not clean enough for salad. Pay attention to container exteriors and refrigerator handles too. Keeping gloves on while moving from raw meat to plating is no substitute for separating tasks and equipment.
paragraphs.scenario: Raw fish is on an upper refrigerator shelf and finished desserts below it. Check that the fish container has a lid and is not leaking, and rearrange it according to the restaurant’s separation system. If a leak has occurred, also report any affected food.

rst-1-hyg-07.summary: Control food separation, dripping juices, and routes through hands and utensils together.
rst-1-hyg-07.activity: Draw refrigerator shelves and a preparation counter, and show where raw meat, washed vegetables, and finished dishes belong, explaining why.

rst-1-hyg-08.title: Clean and disinfect utensils and manage chemicals
rst-1-hyg-08.objective: Remove dirt before appropriate disinfection, and prevent chemical mix-ups.

paragraphs.knowledge: Cleaning removes dirt; disinfection and microbial killing address microorganisms. Applying chemicals while dirt remains may fail to produce the expected effect. Select a method suited to the utensil’s material and purpose, and complete drying and clean storage as well.
paragraphs.procedure: Remove visible dirt, wash with detergent, and rinse thoroughly under running water. Treat with the specified heat or chemical method, then dry and store. Put chemicals into labelled, dedicated containers, check the instructions and concentration, and return them to the designated location away from food.
paragraphs.mistakes: Transferring chemicals into empty beverage containers or using unlabelled bottles can lead to incorrect use. Do not mix chemicals on your own judgment. Wiping disinfected utensils with a dirty cloth can contaminate them again.
paragraphs.scenario: After disinfecting a cutting board, you find dirt near its handle. Start again from cleaning before marking it as disinfected. Do not add more chemical to hide the dirt; review the procedure and checking method too.

rst-1-hyg-08.summary: Do not skip cleaning, rinsing, appropriate treatment, drying, or storage; distinguish chemicals clearly.
rst-1-hyg-08.activity: Imagine checking the label of a chemical used at the restaurant. Create a checklist covering purpose, concentration, storage location, and prohibited actions.

rst-1-hyg-09.title: Clean toilets without carrying contamination into the kitchen
rst-1-hyg-09.objective: Separate cleaning tools and worn items, and clean contact surfaces as well.

paragraphs.knowledge: Toilet seats, flush levers, doorknobs, and handrails may carry contamination that cannot be seen. Cleaning only the bowl is insufficient if hand-contact surfaces remain dirty. It is important not to mix toilet tools with kitchen tools.
paragraphs.procedure: Prepare clothing, footwear, gloves, and dedicated tools separate from those for cooking. Clean and disinfect contact surfaces, handwashing facilities, the bowl, and the floor according to the designated procedure. Wash the tools used, dry and store them, and wash hands thoroughly after finishing. Leave a record of the check.
paragraphs.mistakes: Touching doors and kitchen handles one after another with cleaning gloves spreads contamination. Do not take toilet brushes to other locations or skip handwashing after cleaning. Use the specified chemicals suited to the place and material.
paragraphs.scenario: You are called from the kitchen during cleaning. Do not return to cooking wearing the cleaning gloves. Pause the cleaning safely and put the tools away. Complete preparation for returning to cooking and wash hands; discuss a change of worker if needed.

rst-1-hyg-09.summary: Use dedicated items, clean hand-contact areas too, and wash hands thoroughly after finishing.
rst-1-hyg-09.activity: Explain the sequence from toilet cleaning to returning to cooking, including why each step prevents contamination from spreading.

rst-1-hyg-10.title: Check health, wounds, and work clothing before starting
rst-1-hyg-10.objective: Check your health and appearance and report any problem that may affect food without hiding it.

paragraphs.knowledge: Diarrhea, vomiting, hand wounds, dirty clothing, and jewelry can lead to food contamination or foreign matter. Reporting your health is part of the job too. Wearing gloves does not compensate for illness or insufficient handwashing.
paragraphs.procedure: Before starting, check your health, hands, hair, and clothing. If you have symptoms, tell the person in charge before entering food preparation and obtain instructions on medical consultation or work. Report wounds and confirm the necessary protection or reassignment. Wear clean clothing and remove jewelry.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not handle food while hiding symptoms because the restaurant is short-staffed. Infection may occur without symptoms, so daily handwashing remains essential. If you use an adhesive dressing, protect and check it so that it cannot fall into food.
paragraphs.scenario: You have been vomiting repeatedly since just before leaving for work. Do not decide by yourself that it is just fatigue. Report the symptoms and when they began. Rather than entering the workplace and continuing to cook, follow the person in charge’s instructions.

rst-1-hyg-10.summary: Report symptoms early and check clean clothing and wound management before working.
rst-1-hyg-10.activity: Practice what to tell the person in charge in two cases: having diarrhea and having a wound on a finger.

rst-2-hyg-06.title: Judge abnormalities in water used at the restaurant
rst-2-hyg-06.objective: Understand controls suited to the water source and equipment, and direct suspension and reporting when a problem occurs.

paragraphTitles.mistakes: Clear water is not necessarily safe
paragraphTitles.scenario: When water is cloudy before opening

paragraphs.knowledge: Water used for cooking or food must be tap water or water suitable for drinking. Required inspections vary depending on whether water comes directly from the public supply, through a receiving tank, or from a well. The person in charge checks the restaurant’s source, storage facilities, and presence of disinfection or purification equipment, and understands the applicable controls.
paragraphs.procedure: Before opening, check and record color, cloudiness, and odor. Schedule water-quality tests, tank cleaning, and equipment inspections at the intervals required for the restaurant, and retain certificates and results. Use a method that checks the water actually reaching food, such as sampling at the tap used for cooking.
paragraphs.mistakes: Clear appearance does not rule out contamination from a disaster or equipment fault. If unusual odor, cloudiness, or suspected contamination after a disaster is found, do not taste the water to check it or decide on your own that boiling is enough. Stop using it, identify effects on food, ice, and utensils, and consult the public health center or the person responsible for the system.
paragraphs.scenario: The morning after heavy rain, tap water is cloudy. The person in charge stops cooking and ice-making and checks when water was already used and for which food. They select work that can continue with a verified safe alternative water supply and arrange tests and equipment inspection. They retain the findings and basis for restarting before informing staff.

rst-2-hyg-06.summary: Know the restaurant’s water source; stop using it when abnormalities arise and check the affected scope and conditions for restarting.
rst-2-hyg-06.activity: Read for 8 minutes; draw the route from water source to tap in 7 minutes. Spend 8 minutes preparing instructions after cloudiness is discovered and a plan for alternative operations. Explain items to check in testing records for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-07.title: Remove the sources of rodents and insects
rst-2-hyg-07.objective: Prevent pests according to their type and entry routes, and revise measures using inspection findings.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: Do not focus only on the one pest you saw
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Applying chemicals does not necessarily solve the problem
paragraphTitles.scenario: Small flies increase in the same place

paragraphs.knowledge: Some flies enter from outside while others breed in drains and similar places. Cockroaches hide around warm equipment, dark gaps, and places with water or food residue. Rodents enter through gaps around pipes or ceilings. Preventing food contamination and foreign matter requires combined control of food sources, water, hiding places, and entry points.
paragraphs.procedure: Record capture locations and discovery times, and inspect drainage, food storage, screens, and doors where numbers have increased. Cover opened products and keep them off floors and away from walls. Consult specialists as needed and plan preventive control or suitable extermination based on the investigation. After treatment, check that dead pests and chemicals cannot contaminate food.
paragraphs.mistakes: Spraying insecticide near food during preparation causes another form of contamination. An insect-attracting light visible from outside may also draw pests indoors. Do not just add more traps: first check repairs to entry points, drain cleaning, and waste storage, then confirm chemical-use conditions and conditions for restarting.
paragraphs.scenario: Insects keep appearing at the washing area despite nightly extermination. The person in charge uses capture records to focus the investigation around the drains and finds an underside of a cover that had not been cleaned. They revise cleaning instructions and monitor occurrences for several days. If there is no improvement, they investigate equipment gaps and specialist measures.

rst-2-hyg-07.summary: Use pest discovery records to remove breeding sources and address entry points.
rst-2-hyg-07.activity: Read for 8 minutes; classify entry points and breeding sources in the restaurant for 7 minutes. Use hypothetical capture data to choose priority locations in 8 minutes, then explain measures that do not contaminate food for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-08.title: Manage waste and wastewater
rst-2-hyg-08.objective: Standardize sorting, storage, and removal of waste and prevent contamination by dirty water.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: The restaurant is responsible for its waste
paragraphTitles.procedure: Assign responsibility through the end of removal
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Do not end cleanup at transport alone
paragraphTitles.scenario: When collection is delayed by one day

paragraphs.knowledge: The business is responsible for managing appropriate disposal of waste from its activities. Follow local authority and contracted collector rules for waste categories and removal. Food-waste liquids and leftover drinks attract insects and rodents, while dirty water can contaminate clean areas. Include waste containers and drainage facilities in the hygiene plan.
paragraphs.procedure: Provide covered, easy-to-clean containers and drain food waste so it does not leak. Sort bottles, cans, and other items as required. Keep storage away from food, and check containers and lids for dirt and damage after collection. Route wastewater through the proper equipment rather than discharging it directly onto floors or outside the facility.
paragraphs.mistakes: Carrying bags away does not finish the task if dirty containers and floors remain as a source of pests. Pressing waste bags down with hands or feet also risks injury from sharp fragments. Plan for collection days that coincide with holidays and arrange capacity, storage locations, and communication with the collector in advance.
paragraphs.scenario: The collector reports a one-day delay. The supervisor checks spare capacity in covered containers and the storage location and separates food waste and recyclables properly. Rather than temporarily leaving waste in passageways, they check leaks and odor and assign removal duties during business hours. Records include cleaning after collection and the condition of containers.

rst-2-hyg-08.summary: Manage sorting through to cleaning containers after collection as one process.
rst-2-hyg-08.activity: Read for 8 minutes; organize sorting and collection rules for 7 minutes, then prepare an alternative process for collection delays in 8 minutes. Check routes that keep dirty water out of clean areas for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-09.title: Support health reporting and hygienic behavior
rst-2-hyg-09.objective: Avoid assigning unwell staff to food preparation, arrange substitutes, and direct prevention of recontamination.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: A workplace that makes reporting easy helps prevention
paragraphTitles.mistakes: Gloves and stool tests are not universal protection
paragraphTitles.scenario: A cook contacts you before opening

paragraphs.knowledge: Food handlers with diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or similar symptoms do not engage in food preparation. Check fever, hand wounds or infected wounds, and family members’ health as needed. Infection can be symptom-free, so health checks alone do not establish safety. A system that maintains clothing rules, handwashing, and separation of tasks is necessary.
paragraphs.procedure: Check health before the shift and determine contacts and substitutes for problems. Hats cover hair, and masks cover both nose and mouth. Use separate footwear for the kitchen and toilet, for example. Put gloves on after washing hands, and change them when moving from contaminated work to clean work or when damaged. Do not skip handwashing when changing gloves either.
paragraphs.mistakes: Touching everything with gloves spreads contamination through their surfaces. Having regular stool tests does not rule out later health changes or asymptomatic infection. Do not make staff hide symptoms because of understaffing; the person in charge receives the report and decides on a safe reassignment.
paragraphs.scenario: A cook reports vomiting since the previous night. The person in charge does not choose the option of having them come in only to plate food; they stop the worker from food preparation and arrange a substitute. They check the previous day’s work and contacts and proceed with necessary cleaning and consultation. Return to work is judged according to advice from a medical institution or similar source and the restaurant’s procedure.

rst-2-hyg-09.summary: Manage symptom reporting, exclusion from food preparation, replacement assignments, and daily hygienic behavior together.
rst-2-hyg-09.activity: Read for 8 minutes; create questions for a health report in 7 minutes and practice redistributing roles after an absence in 8 minutes. Explain situations requiring glove changes and handwashing for 7 minutes.

rst-2-hyg-10.title: Keep allergen information up to date
rst-2-hyg-10.objective: Track ingredient changes and possible cross-contact, and explain uncertainties to customers without making unsupported claims.

paragraphTitles.knowledge: A dish name is not enough to judge
paragraphTitles.scenario: The usual sauce is out of stock

paragraphs.knowledge: Allergens may be present not only in main ingredients but also in seasonings, sauces, and processed products. Consider unintended cross-contact through shared utensils or boiling vessels. Distinguish labelling on packaged processed foods from information provided about dishes served in the restaurant, and check current official information for changes in the labelling system.
paragraphs.procedure: For each menu item, compare ingredients with labels on purchased products and record the change date and checker. When changing suppliers or recipes, update the kitchen, service staff, and customer information materials at the same time. Staff receiving questions check current materials and the person in charge, and clearly explain possible cross-contact that cannot be excluded through shared equipment or similar factors.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not guarantee safety because an ingredient is not visible, was not used previously, or is present only in a small amount. Possible cross-contact may remain even after removing the ingredient. When uncertain, explain that checks are in progress and hold the service decision. Also train staff in emergency reporting and their roles if symptoms occur.
paragraphs.scenario: Just before a substitute sauce is used, the supervisor notices a difference on its label. They stop giving the existing dish information and update the recipe and customer explanation. Tables that have already ordered are told of the change. For a customer who asked about allergies, the person in charge checks individually before deciding the response.

rst-2-hyg-10.summary: Keep ingredient changes, actual kitchen practice, and information materials aligned; do not declare unresolved issues safe.
rst-2-hyg-10.activity: Read for 8 minutes; list all places needing updates when introducing a substitute sauce in 7 minutes. Practice answers to customer questions and explanations of possible cross-contact for 8 minutes, and check staff roles in emergency communication for 7 minutes.

rst-1-hyg-11.title: When to wash hands and where cleaning is often missed
rst-1-hyg-11.objective: Wash hands when changing tasks, including fingertips, thumbs and other easily missed areas.

paragraphs.knowledge: Handwashing reduces microorganisms that could transfer to food as well as removing visible dirt. Task changes matter: after using the toilet, before entering the kitchen, after handling raw meat or fish, after cleaning, and after touching money. Gloves do not remove the need to wash hands.
paragraphs.procedure: Wet your hands under running water and use soap to wash the palms, backs of the hands, between the fingers, around the base of each thumb, fingertips and wrists. Rinse thoroughly and dry hygienically. Follow the shop’s procedure for repeated washing or disinfection, and avoid touching dirty surfaces again.
paragraphs.mistakes: Briefly rubbing only the palms or drying with a dirty towel is insufficient. Simply spraying alcohol onto wet hands does not replace washing with soap and running water. Rings and long nails hinder cleaning and foreign-object prevention.
paragraphs.scenario: After helping at the till, you are about to return directly to shaping rice balls. Wash your hands first and change to new gloves if necessary. Even if your hands look clean, consider what you touched and what task comes next.

rst-1-hyg-11.summary: Remember both where and when to wash, and avoid contaminating your hands again after drying.
rst-1-hyg-11.activity: Slowly demonstrate handwashing and check each other’s thumbs, fingertips and spaces between the fingers.

rst-1-hyg-12.title: 5S, cleaning schedules and waste handling
rst-1-hyg-12.objective: Carry out tidying and planned cleaning, and manage waste separately from food.

paragraphs.knowledge: Combine sorting to identify necessary items, arranging designated storage places, removing dirt, maintaining cleanliness and building the habit of following procedures. In addition to daily cleaning, schedule periodic work such as cleaning inside refrigerators and drainage equipment.
paragraphs.procedure: Check your assigned area and timing, and protect food before cleaning. Put food waste in dedicated containers with lids and keep them in designated places that do not obstruct work. Separate combustible waste, bottles, cans, used oil and other waste according to local and shop rules.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not stop after sweeping the visible floor; inspect places where dirt accumulates too. Leaving waste containers open can attract insects and rodents. Waste from pufferfish processing requires special management and must not be mixed with ordinary food waste.
paragraphs.scenario: The drains are due for cleaning, but the shop is busy and no one has been assigned. Do not assume someone else will do it; check with the person in charge. Avoid overlapping with food handling and arrange for the completed work to be checked.

rst-1-hyg-12.summary: Set storage locations, cleaning frequencies and waste categories, and follow them to maintain cleanliness.
rst-1-hyg-12.activity: Imagine a kitchen and create daily, weekly and monthly cleaning schedules and a waste-sorting chart.

rst-1-hyg-13.title: The HACCP approach and dishes served without heating
rst-1-hyg-13.objective: Classify dishes by their preparation processes and manage temperature and time until serving for unheated dishes.

paragraphs.knowledge: The HACCP approach identifies where hazards arise in a process and what needs checking. Grouping dishes into those served without heating, those heated then served, and those involving heating and cooling reveals differences in key control points. Unheated dishes have no final heating step.
paragraphs.procedure: Check the menu’s preparation processes. For unheated dishes, verify ingredient receiving, washing, equipment cleanliness and cold storage. Take out only the required amount of salad or similar food and plate it just before serving. If it must wait, refrigerate it according to the shop’s control plan and keep the serving time in mind.
paragraphs.mistakes: Do not decide the whole process from the name “salad” alone. If boiled ingredients are cooled before mixing, cooling must also be controlled. Unheated does not mean that disinfection or temperature control is unnecessary. Avoid leaving plated dishes at room temperature for a long time.
paragraphs.scenario: You prepared salads early for a group, but the guests are delayed. Instead of leaving the plates on the serving counter, check storage conditions and elapsed time and consult the person in charge. Change to a method that maintains safe control.

rst-1-hyg-13.summary: Classify by the process, not just the dish name, and protect food with no final heating step from contamination and rising temperatures.
rst-1-hyg-13.activity: Write the preparation processes for sashimi, grilled fish and soup that is cooled, then compare their control points.

rst-1-hyg-14.title: Check that heat has reached the centre of the food
rst-1-hyg-14.objective: Connect heating methods with checking the food’s centre, and stop serving if heating is insufficient.

paragraphs.knowledge: Heating requires attention to heat reaching the centre, not just surface browning. For bacterial control in meat, the source gives a centre temperature of 75℃ for at least 1 minute. Requirements differ by food and hazard, so the same figures do not apply to every dish.
paragraphs.procedure: Cook the specified sizes and quantities, following validated heat settings, times and procedures. Where needed, use a probe thermometer to check the centre. If the standard is not met, stop serving and obtain instructions such as further heating. Plate with clean utensils and record the results.
paragraphs.mistakes: The set temperature of frying oil or an oven is different from the temperature at the centre of the food. Do not measure only the surface with infrared equipment and assume the centre is the same. For bivalve shellfish and similar foods at risk of norovirus contamination, the source specifies a centre temperature of 85〜90℃ for at least 90 seconds. Distinguish the relevant foods and check the shop’s plan.
paragraphs.scenario: Someone cooks meat of different thicknesses for the same time and is about to skip the centre check. The usual cooking time does not necessarily ensure safety; follow the checking procedure. Do not serve it while claiming it is thoroughly cooked before this has been confirmed.

rst-1-hyg-14.summary: Distinguish equipment settings from the food’s centre temperature, and hygienically serve dishes that have been checked.
rst-1-hyg-14.activity: Explain how to prepare, measure with, check and clean a probe thermometer after use, including how centre temperature differs from the set temperature.

rst-1-hyg-15.title: Link cooling and reheating safely
rst-1-hyg-15.objective: Understand the danger of leaving cooked food uncontrolled, and connect cooling, storage and reheating records.

paragraphs.knowledge: For curry, soup and other dishes stored after cooking, cooling is also important. The source describes 10〜60℃ as a danger temperature zone. Plan and control the sequence of heating, cooling, refrigeration and reheating to avoid keeping food in this range for a long time.
paragraphs.procedure: Prepare clean cooling containers and equipment beforehand. After cooking, cool promptly using the shop’s method, for example by adjusting quantity or depth, and check time and temperature. Maintain specified storage conditions, and when reheating, check that the centre has received the required heating.
paragraphs.mistakes: Leaving a large pot at room temperature overnight is not proper cooling. Simply putting it in a refrigerator does not guarantee that its centre has cooled. The source includes cooling-time examples with different applications and references; do not mix the figures. Use the validated plan adopted by the shop.
paragraphs.scenario: Soup for the next day is still warm after the planned cooling time. Check container size and equipment use, and report the actual time and temperature to the person in charge. Do not alter the record to show the planned values.

rst-1-hyg-15.summary: Cooling is an important step before storage. Record measured times and temperatures, and do not hide deviations.
rst-1-hyg-15.activity: Create a process chart for serving soup the following day, with checks for the start of cooling, measurement, storage and reheating.

rst-1-week01-q01.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q01.stem: A staple has come loose near a dish. Which hazard should you consider?
options: Bacterial growth only
Insufficient sugar
Metal fragments entering the food
Loss of vitamins
rst-1-week01-q01.explanation: Metal fragments are a physical hazard that can cause injury if they enter food. Check nearby food and locate the staple, then report it.

rst-1-week01-q02.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q02.stem: What is the problem with using raw-meat tongs to plate cooked meat too?
options: They may transfer bacteria to cooked food
The meat’s weight will always increase
The plating temperature will always drop
All fat will melt
rst-1-week01-q02.explanation: Even if heating reduces bacteria, raw-meat utensils can contaminate the food again. Use separate utensils for each purpose.

rst-1-week01-q03.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q03.stem: What is the main purpose of taking cold ingredients out in small batches while working?
options: To leave them at room temperature for longer
To make packaging easier to tear
To extend the use-by date
To shorten the time outside cold temperature control
rst-1-week01-q03.explanation: Taking out only what is needed reduces time left at room temperature. The purpose is not to extend the date.

rst-1-week01-q04.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q04.stem: Which is appropriate when handling raw chicken to control Campylobacter?
options: Serve it raw without conditions if fresh
Heat thoroughly and prevent contamination of other food
Make heating unnecessary by marinating in seasonings
Serve after only cooling the surface
rst-1-week01-q04.explanation: Campylobacter is a concern in chicken and similar foods. Freshness or seasoning alone cannot guarantee safety.

rst-1-week01-q05.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q05.stem: What should you be aware of when soil attached to rice, beans, or similar ingredients is brought into the kitchen?
options: Food contamination by microorganisms found in nature
All soil is sterile
The presence of soil makes disinfection unnecessary
Soil can be mixed directly into food if dry
rst-1-week01-q05.explanation: Soil can contain microorganisms such as Bacillus cereus. Hygienic control of ingredients and work areas is necessary.

rst-1-week01-q06.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q06.stem: A storage problem is found when receiving red-fleshed fish. Why must you not assume cooking alone solves it?
options: Fish always becomes poisonous when heated
Refrigeration always increases toxins
Some hazards, such as histamine, are not resolved by heating
Soy sauce can always remove the hazard
rst-1-week01-q06.explanation: Effective measures vary by hazard. Do not accept a hazard from improper storage simply because cooking is planned.

rst-1-week01-q07.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q07.stem: The product name and quantity match the delivery note. What check is needed next?
options: Finish receiving inspection without opening anything if the quantity matches
Quality, including packaging, dates and storage conditions
Recheck only the prices on the delivery note
Skip checking the temperature if the delivery address is correct
rst-1-week01-q07.explanation: Receiving inspection requires checking the actual product’s quality and storage conditions as well as matching the paperwork.

rst-1-week01-q08.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-1-week01-q08.stem: An ingredient arrives with an unreadable date label. What is the appropriate action?
options: Copy the date from the same product
Write the receiving date as the expiry date
Remove the packaging and discard the date label
Confirm with the person in charge or supplier before deciding acceptance
rst-1-week01-q08.explanation: Do not leave an unconfirmed date unresolved or label it by guesswork. Obtain accurate information.

rst-2-week01-q01.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q01.stem: A hygiene plan was stamped “checked” before the work began. What corrective action should the person in charge take?
options: Make advance stamping the official method
Treat additional stamps as proof of safety
Teach checking and recording at the time of the actual work and verify what happens
Remove the forms and rely only on verbal promises
rst-2-week01-q01.explanation: Records must be based on actual checks. Stamping in advance makes it impossible to establish whether control was carried out.

rst-2-week01-q02.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q02.stem: More cleaning tools were added, but they are not separated by area and are shared with contaminated areas. What is the improvement?
options: Separate purposes and storage locations and train staff to use the tools accordingly
Use the same tools in a different order
Increase only the number of tools again
Do not separate them until dirt becomes visible
rst-2-week01-q02.explanation: Clarify purposes, storage, and treatment after use, not just the number of tools, to prevent contamination across areas.

rst-2-week01-q03.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q03.stem: A worker wants to replace a grease-cleaning product with an acidic cleaner without authorization. What is the appropriate judgment?
options: Assume all cleaners have the same effect
Choose the one with a strong smell
Mix chemicals to increase the effect
Choose after checking the dirt, material, and product’s intended use
rst-2-week01-q03.explanation: Use cleaners according to the nature of the dirt, utensil material, and product label. Mixing on your own judgment is dangerous.

rst-2-week01-q04.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q04.stem: Detergent and disinfectant are being transferred into beverage bottles. What should the person in charge do?
options: Allow it if staff remember the colors
Correct this by using labelled, dedicated containers that prevent accidental drinking and misuse
Put them in the food refrigerator to distinguish them
Remove labels to make their appearance uniform
rst-2-week01-q04.explanation: Manage chemicals with containers, labels, and storage locations that prevent confusion with food. Do not rely on verbal memory alone.

rst-2-week01-q05.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q05.stem: Disinfected utensils are being returned to a shelf with dirty hands. Which improvement takes priority?
options: Review hygienic handling and storage after disinfection
Unconditionally increase only the chemical concentration
Change only the shelf’s appearance
Only add more records of disinfection time
rst-2-week01-q05.explanation: Cleanliness cannot be maintained if recontamination occurs after disinfection. Manage removal, hands, and storage locations together.

rst-2-week01-q06.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q06.stem: Items placed in the handwashing area have made it unusable. What is appropriate facility management?
options: Allow staff to wipe hands at another counter
Skip handwashing until the items are removed
Restore immediate usability and include it in daily checks
Hide the handwashing-area sign
rst-2-week01-q06.explanation: Handwashing facilities must be usable when needed. Include obstructions and missing supplies in inspections too.

rst-2-week01-q07.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q07.stem: A worker returned a thermometer that failed calibration to its original place. What prevents reuse?
options: Have just one person remember it is faulty
Identify it as unusable, isolate it, and manage a replacement
Replace the display with a normal reading
Change only its storage location every day
rst-2-week01-q07.explanation: Identification and isolation are needed to keep failed instruments out of use, together with a reliable replacement.

rst-2-week01-q08.objective: Apply the hygiene knowledge from week 1 according to the situation.
rst-2-week01-q08.stem: A report says the water has an unusual color. What should the person in charge decide first?
options: Keep using it for cooking if the color is faint
Hide the color with seasoning
Do not record it until the abnormality disappears
Stop using it and investigate the cause and affected scope
rst-2-week01-q08.explanation: Abnormal water affects food and washing too. Do not hide its appearance; suspend use until safety is confirmed.
